units.title: The Lymphatic System
units.intro:
Capillaries leak fluid into tissues (tissue fluid). Most returns to blood capillaries; the rest becomes **lymph** and is collected by lymph vessels that have valves and pass through **nodes** (filters packed with white cells). Lymph returns to blood near the collarbone veins. Also carries fat from villi (lacteals).

Compared with blood: no red cells, no high-pressure pump — muscles and valves squeeze lymph along. Nodes swell when they are fighting infection.

cards.title: More detail — lymph
body: Tissue fluid is plasma minus most large proteins. At the arterial end of a capillary, pressure pushes fluid out; at the venous end some is sucked back. The leftover is lymph. Vessels start blind-ended, have valves, pass nodes (armpit, neck, groin, mesentery). Spleen and thymus are related lymphoid organs (thymus trains T-cells — Grade 11).
If lymph drainage fails, the limb swells (oedema). After a fatty meal the lymph from the gut looks milky because of lacteals.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Lymph
body: Lymph is a colourless fluid containing water, waste materials, cell products (such as hormones and enzymes), digested fat, lymphocytes and phagocytes, which is transported from the blood capillaries by diffusion and filtration.
Rising osmotic pressure of the tissue fluid interferes with osmotic reabsorption of water in the blood capillaries.
The volume and pressure of fluid in the interstitial spaces then tends to increase.
Once tissue fluid enters the lymphatic vessels, it becomes lymph.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Lymphatic Vessels
body: The lymphatic vessels are formed by the lymphatic capillaries, which unite before entering either the thoracic ducts or right lymphatic duct.
The walls of the lymphatic capillaries, like those of the blood capillaries, consist of a single layer of squamous epithelial cells, but are thinner.
The lining of the small intestine contains specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals.
The larger lymphatic vessels lead to specialized organs called lymph nodes.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Lymph Nodes
body: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing large numbers of leukocytes.
Generally, they occur in groups or chains along the paths of the larger lymphatic vessels throughout the body, but are absent in the central nervous system.
Cervical region: nodes in the cervical region occur along the lower border of the mandible, in front of and behind the ears, and deep within the neck along the paths of larger blood vessels.
Axillary region: nodes in the underarm region (armpit) receive lymph from vessels that drain the upper limbs, wall of the thorax, mammary glands (breasts) and upper wall of the abdomen.

lessons.title: Comparison between the Lymphatic System and the Circulatory System

cards.title: 3.2 Comparison between the Lymphatic System and the Circulatory System
body: The circulatory and lymphatic systems are two different systems.
The function of the circulatory system is to transport nutrients, oxygen and other useful substances.
The system is also used to remove waste substances, such as carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes produced by cells.
The function of the lymphatic system is to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces.
The substances that leak from the capillaries are collected and returned to the blood circulation by the lymphatic system.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: Lymphatic system does not include  A) lymph nodes.  B) spleen.  C) thymus.  D) adrenal glands.  E) lymph vessels.

steps.text: **Step 1.** The lymphatic system includes lymph nodes, lymph vessels, the spleen, and the thymus gland, all of which play roles in immunity. **Adrenal glands** are part of the endocrine system and produce hormones like adrenaline and cortisol; they are not part of the lymphatic system.

glossary.meaning: Lymph is a colourless fluid containing water, waste materials, cell products (such as hormones and enzymes), digested fat, lymphocytes and phagocytes, which is transported from the blood capillaries by diffusion and filtration.
Blood is a fluid tissue that flows in the circulatory system.

tips.text: The lymphatic system is a system consisting of different organs and tissue.
The lymph contains solutes that pass from the blood capillaries. These include ions, nutrients, gases and some proteins; and cell products such as hormones, enzymes and waste products.

The lymphatic system performs the following functions: it helps to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial space, absorbs and transport fat into the blood circulation, and helps in defending the body against diseasecausing agents (as part of the immune system).
The lymph nodes are located at intervals along the lymph and are called lymph glands.
Tonsils form a protective ring of lymphatic tissue around the opening between the nasal and oral cavities. They provide protection against infection in the nose and mouth.
The spleen helps to remove iron from the haemoglobin of the old red blood cells and also produces antibodies against harmful organisms.
The thymus gland plays an important role in the development of the immune response in early life. It is a site of lymphocyte formation and antibody production.
How are nutrients, oxygen and other useful substances transported to all the body’s cells? 2.
How do you think the waste substances produced by each cell are removed?
The circulatory and lymphatic systems are two different systems. Both, however, are involved in the transportation of materials.

questions.q:
Complete the following paragraph using the terms that fit the unit (write the two missing terms in order):

The walls of lymphatic capillaries are made of thin, ____________ endothelial cells that work like one-way swing doors [96, 97]. Because the lymphatic system has no pump of its own [95, 101, 103, 104], lymph is pushed slowly toward the heart by the squeezing action of nearby skeletal muscles, by breathing movements, and by ____________ along all lymphatic vessels that prevent backflow [88, 96, 103, 104].
questions.answer: overlapping ; valves
why: **Recall the wall structure of lymphatic capillaries.** The unit states that lymphatic vessel walls are made of thin, overlapping endothelial cells that act like one-way swing doors: when tissue-fluid pressure outside is high they swing open, and when fluid tries to leave they swing shut, locking the fluid in as lymph [96, 97].

**Recall how lymph is propelled without a pump.** The lymphatic system has no pump [95, 101, 103, 104]. Lymph moves through the massaging action of skeletal muscles, breathing movements, and one-way valves present along all lymphatic vessels, which close if fluid tries to flow backward [88, 96, 103, 104].

**Fill the blanks in order.** First blank: the cells are described as overlapping (not ciliated, not muscular). Second blank: the anti-backflow structures mentioned in the unit are valves. The paragraph therefore reads: overlapping endothelial cells ... and valves along all lymphatic vessels.

**Check the completed sentence.** The completed paragraph now correctly links structure (overlapping endothelial cells producing one-way entry) with mechanism of flow (skeletal muscle squeeze, breathing, and one-way valves), matching the unit exactly [88, 96, 103, 104].

questions.q:
Complete the following paragraph (write the two missing terms in order):

Lymphatic capillaries are microscopic, ____________ capillaries that begin as dead-ends inside the tissues rather than forming a loop [87, 95, 97]. When the pressure of tissue fluid around them rises, fluid pushes the overlapping endothelial cells inward and enters; once inside it becomes ____________, a colourless watery fluid that lacks red blood cells and platelets [87, 95, 103].
questions.answer: closed-ended ; lymph
why: **Identify the capillary shape.** The unit describes lymphatic capillaries as microscopic, closed-ended capillaries that merge into larger vessels and start as dead-ends in the tissues, unlike the open loops of the circulatory system [87, 95, 97].

**Identify the fluid formed inside.** Once interstitial (tissue) fluid has entered the lymphatic capillary and is locked in by the overlapping cells, it is called lymph: a colourless, watery fluid containing water, leaked proteins, cell products, digested lipids and white blood cells [87, 95].
**Fill the blanks in order.** First blank: closed-ended. Second blank: lymph. The paragraph then reads correctly: lymphatic capillaries are closed-ended ... the fluid becomes lymph.

**Verify against the unit.** Both terms appear in the unit's description of lymph and lymphatic vessels, and the completed sentence keeps the unit's direction of flow (tissue fluid to lymph) intact [87, 95, 96, 97].

By contrast, the spleen is described as the largest lymphatic organ and acts mainly as a filter of ____________ [100, 102].
questions.answer: lacteals ; chyle (and the spleen filters blood)
why: **Identify the intestinal lymphatic capillaries.** The unit names the specialized lymphatic capillaries in the lining of the small intestine lacteals; they absorb digested fats, which are too large to enter blood capillaries directly [86, 94, 97].
**Identify the milky fluid.** Because of its high content of emulsified fat droplets, the lymph in lacteals looks milky-white and is called chyle [86, 94, 97].

**Complete the third blank.** The unit's pro-tip states that lymph nodes filter lymph while the spleen filters blood, so the spleen's role is blood filtration (removing old red blood cells, recycling iron, producing antibodies and storing blood) [100, 102].

**Read the completed paragraph.** The paragraph now reads: intestinal lymphatic capillaries are lacteals, their fatty lymph is chyle, and the spleen filters blood - all directly supported by the unit [86, 94, 97, 100, 102].

questions.q: Large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen sometimes leak from blood capillaries into the tissue spaces. Which statement best explains why these large proteins can enter lymphatic capillaries but cannot re-enter blood capillaries?

options.A: Blood capillaries actively push large proteins back into the blood, but the proteins are too large to be pushed into lymphatic capillaries.
options.B: Blood capillaries have very tiny microscopic pores that block large proteins, while lymphatic capillaries have much larger openings formed by thin, overlapping endothelial cells.
options.C: Large proteins are digested into amino acids in the tissue fluid, absorbed by lymphatic capillaries, and rebuilt as proteins in the blood.
options.D: Large proteins enter lymphatic capillaries only because lymph flows in one direction toward the heart, which pulls them away from blood capillaries.

questions.answer: B
why: **State what limits exchange at blood capillaries.** Blood capillaries have thin walls with very tiny microscopic pores. These pores allow water and small solutes to pass in two-way exchange but are too small for large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, so once leaked these proteins cannot diffuse back into the blood [85, 93, 66, 74, 75].

**State the structural feature of lymphatic capillaries.** Lymphatic capillaries are built from thin, overlapping endothelial cells that form large, flap-like openings. When tissue-fluid pressure rises these flaps swing inward and open, so even large proteins can enter the lymphatic capillary [95, 96, 97].

**Link the two facts to the question.** The deciding factor is the size of the openings: tiny pores in blood capillaries exclude large proteins, whereas the large overlapping-cell openings of lymphatic capillaries admit them. This is why the lymphatic system is essential for returning leaked proteins to the blood and preventing loss of osmotic pressure and severe edema [85, 93, 95].

**Test every option.** A is false: the unit gives no active transport of proteins back into blood, and it states the opposite about lymphatic entry. C is false: lymph contains dissolved proteins that leaked from blood capillaries; there is no digestion-and-rebuilding step in the unit. D is false: one-way lymph flow explains direction of movement, not why a large molecule is able to pass through a wall. Only B states the true structural reason.

**Conclude.** Option B is the only statement supported by the unit, because it correctly contrasts the tiny pores of blood capillaries with the large openings of lymphatic capillaries [85, 93, 95, 96].
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A patient suffering from severe protein deficiency produces too few plasma proteins, so tissue fluid is not drawn back into the blood capillaries efficiently. Which statement best explains why the resulting accumulation of tissue fluid is called edema?
questions.answer: D. Edema is the swelling caused by excess fluid accumulating in the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system normally drains this fluid back to the bloodstream.
why: **Define the starting problem.** Some plasma proteins leak out of blood capillaries and are needed to maintain osmotic pressure; when proteins are lost or scarce, water is not reabsorbed well and collects in the interstitial spaces [75, 85, 93, 95].

**Recall what edema is.** The unit defines edema (swelling) as the flooding that results when leaked tissue fluid is allowed to accumulate in the interstitial spaces instead of being drained away [95].

**Recall the drainage route.** The lymphatic capillaries and vessels collect the excess fluid and large leaked proteins and return them to the venous bloodstream near the heart [85, 93, 95]. If this drainage fails or is overwhelmed, fluid stays in the tissues and swelling appears [95].

**Test every option.** A is false: edema is not a shortage of red blood cells. B is false: edema is not caused by rapid movement of lymph into arteries; lymph enters veins near the heart. C is false: swelling is not the trapping of pathogens inside the blood only. D correctly defines edema as interstitial fluid accumulation normally drained by the lymphatic system.
**Conclude.** Option D is the single defensible answer because it matches the unit's cause (untrained tissue fluid) and the lymphatic system's drainage role [85, 93, 95].
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Blood is a red, viscous tissue that contains red blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins, whereas lymph is a clear or milky fluid. Which statement best describes the cellular content of healthy lymph?
questions.answer: A. Lymph contains white blood cells (phagocytes and lymphocytes) but completely lacks red blood cells and platelets.
why: **Recall the composition of lymph.** The unit describes lymph as a colourless, watery fluid containing water, dissolved leaked proteins, cell products such as hormones and enzymes, digested lipids, and white blood cells - especially lymphocytes and phagocytes [87, 95].
**Recall the composition of blood.** Blood is a red, viscous tissue containing red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen [66, 74, 75].

**Compare the two fluids.** Subtracting the blood list from the lymph list leaves white blood cells present in lymph but red blood cells and platelets completely absent. This is one of the unit's listed differences in fluid composition [87, 95, 103].

**Test every option.** B is false: red blood cells and platelets are absent, not abundant. C is false: platelets are absent from lymph. D is false: large plasma proteins are not the cellular component of lymph, and lymph does contain white blood cells.
**Conclude.** Option A is the only statement consistent with the unit: lymph carries white blood cells only, with no red blood cells and no platelets [87, 95, 103].

questions.q: A patient recovering from a leg injury lies still for 3 hours. Because there is no walking movement to squeeze the lymphatic vessels, excess tissue fluid collects in the leg at a steady rate of $$180\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. A nurse then performs a 20-minute manual lymphatic drainage massage that removes $$75\%$$ of the fluid collected. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces after the massage.
questions.answer: $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.
why: **Identify the principle.** When skeletal muscles do not contract, the massaging action that normally pushes lymph along is lost, so tissue fluid collects in the interstitial spaces [88, 96, 104]. The volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid collected in 3 hours.** Collected fluid $$= 180\ \text{mL/hour} \times 3\ \text{hours} = 540\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the volume removed by the massage.** Removed fluid $$= 75\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL} = 0.75 \times 540 = 405\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 540\ \text{mL} - 405\ \text{mL} = 135\ \text{mL}$$, which is the same as $$25\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL}$$.

**State the result.** After the massage, $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still left in the leg tissues, so the drainage has only partly corrected the accumulation. This remaining fluid is what would be seen as pitting swelling (edema) until normal muscle movement resumes [88, 95, 96, 104].

questions.q: During a long bus journey from Asmara to Massawa, a passenger sits without moving for 4 hours and interstitial fluid accumulates in the ankles at a steady rate of $$160\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. After the journey, 85% of this accumulated fluid is drained away as the passenger walks and the calf muscles squeeze the lymphatic vessels. Calculate the volume of fluid, in millilitres, remaining in the ankle tissues.
questions.answer: $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid remains in the ankle tissues.
why: **Identify the principle.** Lymph has no pump, so prolonged sitting without skeletal muscle contraction allows tissue fluid to collect in the lower limbs, and only muscle movement restores drainage [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid accumulated.** Accumulated fluid $$= 160\ \text{mL/hour} \times 4\ \text{hours} = 640\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the fluid drained.** Drained fluid $$= 85\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL} = 0.85 \times 640 = 544\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 640\ \text{mL} - 544\ \text{mL} = 96\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$15\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL}$$.
**State the result.** About $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still trapped in the ankle tissues after walking, which is why ankles can stay puffy for a while after a long sedentary journey [71, 95, 96].

questions.q: A nurse uses a compression bandage on a patient whose foot is swollen after an infection. Over 2.5 hours, tissue fluid collects in the foot at a steady rate of $$200\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. The bandage and gentle elevation then drain away $$72\%$$ of the collected fluid. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces.
questions.answer: $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.
why: **Identify the principle.** With impaired lymph movement, interstitial fluid accumulates and can be partly removed by external compression together with the muscle and breathing movements that normally drive lymph toward the heart [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid collected.** Collected fluid $$= 200\ \text{mL/hour} \times 2.5\ \text{hours} = 500\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the fluid drained.** Drained fluid $$= 72\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL} = 0.72 \times 500 = 360\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 500\ \text{mL} - 360\ \text{mL} = 140\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$28\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL}$$.
**State the result.** The bandage leaves $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid in the foot tissues, so drainage is incomplete and the swelling only partly subsides [95, 96, 104].

questions.q:
The heart of a healthy adult at rest pumps $$7500\ \text{mL}$$ of blood every minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$2.4\%$$ leaks out of the blood capillaries into the interstitial spaces as tissue fluid, and $$92\%$$ of that leaked fluid is eventually collected and returned to the bloodstream by the lymphatic system [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the total volume of lymph returned to the bloodstream in one day, giving your answer in litres.
(b) The same adult's spleen destroys old, damaged red blood cells at a rate that releases $$30\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and this iron is sent to the red bone marrow for recycling. If each newly manufactured red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], calculate the number of new red blood cells that can be produced in 30 days from the recycled iron.
questions.answer: (a) $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$238.5\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 30 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 2.4\%$$ of $$7500\ \text{mL/min} = 0.024 \times 7500 = 180\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 92\%$$ of $$180\ \text{mL/min} = 0.92 \times 180 = 165.6\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].

**Convert the rate to litres per day.** In one day (24 hours $$= 1440$$ minutes) the volume is $$165.6\ \text{mL/min} \times 1440\ \text{min} = 238464\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$, this is $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L/day}$$ (about $$238.5\ \text{L}$$).
**Find the iron salvaged in 30 days.** Iron per day $$= 30\ \text{mg} = 0.030\ \text{g}$$, so in 30 days the spleen releases $$30 \times 0.030\ \text{g} = 0.90\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of new red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.90\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells. This is the iron recycled to the red bone marrow to manufacture new haemoglobin for developing red blood cells [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** Part (a): roughly 238 litres of lymph per day means the lymphatic system returns a volume comparable to the whole blood plasma volume many times over each day, consistent with continuous capillary leakage [85, 93, 95]. Part (b): $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells in 30 days (about $$1.5 \times 10^{10}$$ cells per day) is a large but plausible replacement rate for a marrow continuously recycling iron from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100].

questions.q:
During hard farm work in the Keren area, a man's heart pumps $$9000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.0\%$$ leaks into the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system returns $$95\%$$ of the leaked fluid to the bloodstream [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned per day, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$25\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100]. If each new red blood cell needs $$2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], how many new red blood cells can his marrow produce in 40 days from this recycled iron?
questions.answer: (a) $$369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$369.4\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 40 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.0\%$$ of $$9000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.030 \times 9000 = 270\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 95\%$$ of $$270\ \text{mL/min} = 0.95 \times 270 = 256.5\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].
**Convert to litres per day.** In 1440 minutes the volume is $$256.5 \times 1440 = 369360\ \text{mL} = 369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day.
**Find the iron salvaged in 40 days.** Iron per day $$= 25\ \text{mg} = 0.025\ \text{g}$$; in 40 days the spleen releases $$40 \times 0.025\ \text{g} = 1.0\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{1.0\ \text{g}}{2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, all built from recycled iron sent to the red bone marrow [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** Heavier exercise increases cardiac output and capillary leakage, so both the leak (270 mL/min) and the returned lymph (about 369 L/day) are larger than in the resting adult, as expected [61, 69, 85, 93]. Part (b) gives $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 40 days, a plausible marrow replacement rate [77, 100].

questions.q:
A Massawa fish-processor works in hot conditions and his heart pumps $$8000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.5\%$$ becomes tissue fluid and the lymphatic system drains $$90\%$$ of it back into the blood [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned in one hour, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$40\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and each new red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77]. How many new red blood cells can be made from the iron salvaged in 15 days?
questions.answer: (a) $$15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour (accept $$15.1\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 15 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.5\%$$ of $$8000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.035 \times 8000 = 280\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 90\%$$ of $$280\ \text{mL/min} = 0.90 \times 280 = 252\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].
**Convert to litres per hour.** In 60 minutes the volume is $$252 \times 60 = 15120\ \text{mL} = 15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour.
**Find the iron salvaged in 15 days.** Iron per day $$= 40\ \text{mg} = 0.040\ \text{g}$$; in 15 days the spleen releases $$15 \times 0.040\ \text{g} = 0.60\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.60\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, produced in the red bone marrow from recycled iron [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** The hourly figure $$15.12\ \text{L/hour}$$ equals about $$363\ \text{L/day}$$, in the same order of magnitude as the resting case after allowing for the larger leak and slightly lower drainage fraction; $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 15 days is consistent with the daily iron release [77, 85, 93, 100].

questions.q:
The thymus gland is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum [100]. It is relatively large in infants but gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

(a) Explain the biological reason why the thymus is large and active in an infant and why it shrinks after puberty [100].
(b) In a particular Eritrean child, the thymus weighs $$44\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and then involutes at a steady rate of $$0.9\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 10 years of involution, and then calculate the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, so it is large and active early in life; once the immune system is fully developed and stocked with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty) its active role declines and it involutes, shrinking as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100]. (b) Mass after 10 years $$= 35\ \text{g}$$, and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass is $$\dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 \approx 20.5\%$$.
why: **State the role of the thymus early in life.** The unit states that the thymus plays an essential role early in life as the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses [100]. It is therefore most active while the immune system is being built up in infancy and childhood.

**Explain the shrinking after puberty.** Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, typically around puberty, the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution, gradually shrinking and being replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].
**Calculate the mass lost over 10 years.** Mass lost $$= 0.9\ \text{g/year} \times 10\ \text{years} = 9\ \text{g}$$ [100].
**Calculate the mass after 10 years.** Mass after involution $$= 44\ \text{g} - 9\ \text{g} = 35\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{\text{mass lost}}{\text{puberty mass}} \times 100 = \dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 = 20.45\% \approx 20.5\%$$.

**State the final result.** After 10 years the thymus weighs $$35\ \text{g}$$, a decrease of about $$20.5\%$$ from its $$44\ \text{g}$$ mass at puberty, matching the unit's statement that the gland shrinks after puberty as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].

questions.q:
(a) Explain why a person who had their thymus removed as a young adult might still fight infections reasonably well, even though the gland has a vital early role [100].
(b) In another child the thymus weighs $$40\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes at a steady rate of $$0.8\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 20 years and the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus's essential role is early in life, where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop; by adulthood the immune system is already fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, so much of its protective capacity persists even after the gland involutes or is removed [100]. (b) Mass after 20 years $$= 24\ \text{g}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.
why: **Recall the thymus's early role.** The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, which is why it is essential early in life and relatively large in infants [100].

**Explain why protection persists later.** Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty), the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution [100]. The mature, long-lived lymphocytes already produced continue to provide immune protection, so infections can still be fought reasonably well after the gland is lost.
**Calculate the mass lost over 20 years.** Mass lost $$= 0.8\ \text{g/year} \times 20\ \text{years} = 16\ \text{g}$$ [100].
**Calculate the mass after 20 years.** Mass after involution $$= 40\ \text{g} - 16\ \text{g} = 24\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.
**State the final result.** The thymus falls from $$40\ \text{g}$$ to $$24\ \text{g}$$, a $$40\%$$ decrease, illustrating the progressive involution described in the unit [100].

questions.q:
(a) Explain how the thymus differs in function from the spleen, even though both are lymphatic organs [100, 102].
(b) A patient's thymus weighs $$36\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes steadily to $$21\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100]. Calculate the yearly rate of mass loss in grams per year and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses early in life [100], whereas the spleen is a blood filter that removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood [100, 102]. (b) Rate of loss $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 \approx 41.7\%$$.
why: **State the thymus's function.** The thymus is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum that serves as the maturation site for T-lymphocytes early in life and gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

**State the spleen's function.** The spleen, the largest lymphatic organ in the upper left abdomen, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood for release during heavy bleeding [100, 102].
**Calculate the mass lost.** Mass lost $$= 36\ \text{g} - 21\ \text{g} = 15\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100].
**Calculate the yearly rate of loss.** Rate $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 = 41.67\% \approx 41.7\%$$.
**State the final result.** The thymus loses $$1.25\ \text{g}$$ each year, a $$41.7\%$$ decrease from its $$36\ \text{g}$$ puberty mass, consistent with the unit's account of involution [100].
